data.instrument:
Interim Report following the Buenos Aires Joint Declaration on Trade and Women's Economic Empowerment leading to the creation of the WTO Informal Working Group on Trade and Gender (IWG)

Date of establishment: 23 September 2020 (WT/L/1095/rev.1)

Ultimate outcome of the Buenos Aires Declaration
data.objective:
1. Sharing our respective experiences relating to policies and programs to encourage women's participation in national and international trade through World Trade Organization (WTO)
information exchanges, as appropriate, and voluntary reporting during the WTO trade policy review process.

2. Sharing best practices for conducting gender-based analysis of trade policies and for the monitoring of their effects.

3. Sharing methods and procedures for the collection of gender-disaggregated data, the use of indicators, monitoring and evaluation methodologies, and the analysis of gender-focused statistics related to trade.

4. Working together in the WTO to remove barriers for women's economic empowerment and increase their participation in trade.

5. Ensuring that Aid for Trade supports tools and know-how for analysing, designing and
implementing more gender-responsive trade policies.
data.description:
The Buenos Aires Joint Declaration on Trade and Women's Economic Empowerment was launched in the margins of the 11th WTO Ministerial Conference in 2017.

The IWG is the ultimate outcome of the Buenos Aires Declaration which supported and led to the creation of the Group in 2020.

The IWG is a WTO informal body where its members work collaboratively and voluntarily in an informal, open, inclusive and transparent working group.

The working group is established following requests from WTO members for a more transparent and structured process for their work on trade and gender

Members wanted to ensure that all WTO members and observers, including those not participating in the Buenos Aires Declaration, have the opportunity to take part in the work, whether they contribute or just observe.

data.description:
Members exchanged ideas on how to further advance their understanding of the links between trade and gender and how to approach trade issues with a “gender lens”.

Following a joint webinar organised by the WTO, ITC and UNCTAD on “Applying Gender Lens to WTO”, experts presented on: Defining the concepts behind “gender lens” including the differences between issues of equality and equity; how to introduce gender to WTO’s work; and how to implement a gender lens when implementing WTO rules and agreements.

Members also welcomed the release of the report by the International Gender Champions Trade Impact Group outlining 32 best practices in trade and gender policy.
data.policy_outcome: Report titled “Delivering on the Buenos Aires Declaration on Trade and Women's Economic Empowerment” which compiles best practices and recommendations on trade and gender ranging from data collection methods to impact assessments of trade agreements, government procurement and financial inclusion tools for women entrepreneurs. The report was produced in collaboration with the Trade Impact Group and supported by Australia.

data.description:
Findings of two UNCTAD regional studies based on African Community and Mercosur.

The study compares regional integration in the Eastern African Community (EAC) and Mercosur, focusing on gender equality. While EAC included gender provisions from the start, Mercosur incorporated them later due to civil society advocacy. Despite these differences, both regions have made progress, though gender gaps persist due to factors like legal enforceability, member country differences, and varying accountability. Economic power does not always align with gender equality leadership. Employment patterns show women are concentrated in low-skill or service sectors, with EAC women still largely in agriculture but shifting toward services. Trade liberalization has had mixed impacts on women’s employment, sometimes expanding low-skill opportunities but not managerial roles. Key lessons emphasize improving women’s access to higher-skill jobs, childcare support, better data collection, sharing best practices from “champion” countries, and ensuring accountability in implementing regional gender commitments.

The Waorani Women's Association, founded in 2005 in the Ecuadorian Amazon, brings together 160 women from 58 communities across Napo, Orellana, and Pastaza, and is led by an elected committee focusing on tourism, land protection, health, gender, and family issues. The association undertakes sustainable projects, including handicrafts from chambira fibre and organic chocolate production, which support the community’s economy, conserve forests like the Yasuní Biosphere Reserve, and preserve cultural heritage while addressing challenges from oil extraction and illegal logging. Supported by international partners and recognized with awards like the UN Equator Prize, the association reinvests all profits into the community and aims to expand its sustainable production and exports to benefit more families.
As a result, the Association started to export its products (chocolate and handmade product from chambira palm fibre) in 2018, mostly to the European market.

Programme combined capacity building programmes, donations, technical and institutional support.

All the income comes back to the communities.

While preserving ecosystem and indigenous culture, the programme focused primarily on building the capacity of small-scale producers of handicrafts.

The Export Promotion Agency provided assistance to facilitate the exports of the entrepreneurs. It identified potential markets and advised on the clients’ needs.

data.instrument:

Statistics methodology
data.objective:
• Inform gender-responsive trade policies

• Better understand the gender impacts of countries' trade policies
data.description:
Provides a structured approach to help governments assess, design, and monitor trade policies to ensure they promote women's economic empowerment.

Key Aspects and Best Practices:

Definition and Scope: While often used interchangeably, sex-disaggregated data usually refers to binary classifications (male/female), whereas gender data may include broader social, cultural, and identity characteristics, including transgender and non-binary identities.

Three-Part Analysis: Examines the, often disparate, impact of trade on women in three distinct roles:
As Workers: Analysing how trade affects employment in different sectors, particularly the high percentage of women in services vs. manufacturing/agriculture.
As Consumers: Evaluating how trade policies affect prices and choices for household goods.
As Entrepreneurs/Business Owners: Identifying barriers women-owned businesses face in accessing international markets.

Systematic Approach: Data should be collected systematically across various sectors (e.g., agriculture, disaster risk, financial services) to ensure that the specific experiences of women and other groups are accurately captured.

Intersectionality: Effective data collection goes beyond a simple male/female binary by incorporating intersecting factors such as age, disability, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status.

Quantitative and Qualitative Data: Combining quantitative metrics with qualitative insights (e.g., in-depth interviews, focus groups) helps to understand why gender disparities exist, rather than just identifying that they do.

Inclusivity and Safety: Data collection should include 'prefer not to say' options and allow for self-identification to ensure inclusivity, while also protecting the privacy and safety of participants.

"These barriers limit how much you can trade online," she added.

data.description:
Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) conducts survey-based research on entrepreneurship and entrepreneurship ecosystems worldwide. GEM is a networked consortium of national country teams primarily associated with academic institutions. GEM is the only global research source that collects data on entrepreneurship directly from individual entrepreneurs. GEM tools and data are, therefore, unique and benefit numerous stakeholder groups. GEM collects data in 115 countries on entrepreneurial behaviour and attitudes and assesses entrepreneurial framework conditions.

The GEM 2020/21 women’s entrepreneurship report examines the key differences and similarities in business stages and ambitions, the structural and cultural factors that influence women’s entrepreneurship and how women entrepreneurs were affected by the COVID-19 pandemic in 43 countries.
data.policy_outcome:
Policy recommendations:

GEM recommends a set of four general actions: i) support growth-oriented women entrepreneurs, ii) support women entrepreneurs in male-dominated sectors and address negative stereotypes about women’s leadership ability, iii) encourage women investors and women-focused investment and iv) develop better policy that directly supports women business owners.

GEM recommends a set of five specific actions for emerging economies: i) sponsor global research and data initiatives in emerging economies to improve quality of data for more effective policy and programming, ii) launch entrepreneurship support programs focused on network connection and empowerment, including creating learning platforms, incubators and accelerators programs, iii) support digital business solutions for remote banking and market access, including expanding access of digital tools for women-led businesses and link to business formalisation processes, iv) introduce sectoral relief policies for the self-employed and small business owners, including through tailored support for sectors of retail and hospitality, personal services, education and healthcare, and v) implement care policies for the self-employed and small business owners, including through support for schools and daycare facilities along with other groups of essential workers in mitigation and vaccination schemes
data.outcome_data:
Key findings:

•An estimated 274 million women globally are involved in business startups of less than 42 months of existence, in addition to 139 million women owners/managers of established businesses and 144 million women informal investors globally – representing 40% of investors in the world.

•Globally, women represent 1 in 3 growth-oriented entrepreneurs worldwide. Women represent 42% of entrepreneurs worldwide but own smaller businesses than men, as only 18% have less than 20 employees.

•Surveys reveal that 36% of women entrepreneurs report selling innovative offerings. Depending on the region, women can be significantly more likely to sell innovative offerings than men. In addition, 31% of women entrepreneurs report high growth expectations, including export interests and 29% report a high rate of export activities.

• There are disparities in data on women entrepreneurs, whether from emerging economies or higher-income countries. Women in emerging countries are more active in entrepreneurship activities, while they own smaller startups. Women entrepreneurs in emerging countries have higher growth expectations, and they offer more innovative products. However, the report shows that women in both emerging and high-income economies have similar export activities.

•Cultural and structural factors contribute to explaining the gender export gaps. Globally, women are much more likely than men to be solopreneurs or hire five or fewer employees. Male-dominated sectors are also more trade-oriented than sectors where women are the most active. The report shows a gender gap in internationalisation. Regardless of the income level, women are more likely than men to trade only in the local market, while they are less likely to integrate the national market and international market. However, women with higher income levels tend to be more represented in international markets than women with lower incomes.

•The report also shows the disproportionate impact of the pandemic on women entrepreneurs. Women are 20% more likely than men to report business closures due to the pandemic (41.9% vs 35.5%). About one in three women reported business closures due to the pandemic in low-income countries compared to two in five women in middle-income countries and almost half of women (45.3%) in high-income countries. Family responsibilities, combined with the sector where women are the most active and the smaller size of women-owned businesses, are three factors explaining the gender gap in business closure.

Key findings of Members' work on women entrepreneurs

•Many more women than men run very small businesses with one to five employees.
•Women entrepreneurs are challenged when it comes to navigating foreign regulations and acquiring the necessary skills to start exporting.
•The promising opportunities for women are digital trade and the fact that countries have increasingly begun pursuing policies that support women exporters.
•Trade facilitation measures have the potential to reduce high trade costs weighing on small-sized firms.
•Digital tools help women to operate a business more effectively and efficiently and enable them to establish their business in a foreign market.
•Hidden costs exist in e-commerce operations such as trading in different currencies which requires specific financial skills. Additional costs include: electronic and online payment systems; shipping and safe packaging costs; website maintenance; and data protection costs. "Trading vast amounts of goods that require palletizing and containers raises compliance issues with various export markets, for instance regarding packaging regulations".
•The role of large companies play an important role in prioritizing the inclusion of women entrepreneurs within their supply chains and the need to improve digital trade facilitation. However, working with large corporations proved more difficult on supply chains diversity as it is challenging to find enough women entrepreneurs who are ready to meet the standards and demands in terms of volume, price, and quality. Dedicated programmes exist supporting women entrepreneurs access to GVCs, such as the UPS ITC Women Exporters Program (WEP) which supported between 2018 and 2022, more than 38,000 women entrepreneurs and small business owners worldwide to navigate the export process enabling them to expand their reach, grow their revenues, hire more employees and invest in their families and local communities.
•Women exporters face major difficulties in accessing trade finance
•Women's employment growth in services outshines that of men over the last 20-30 years. However, women-owned services firms export much less than men-owned firms, as women entrepreneurs mostly operate in the least-traded services sectors such as education, health and social work activities. The outlook is however positive as technical barriers to services trade are coming down rapidly, especially in sectors that employ more women, notably thanks to digitalization.
•Women entrepreneurs have suffered a triple financial shock during the COVID-19 pandemic, whose impacts still persist today. Existing regional trade agreements provide several policy solutions to these barriers, such as positive discrimination-based measures in favour of women businesses, provisions enhancing women's access to finance, and those seeking to increase women's access to digital learning and e-commerce. However, most gender provisions do not address women as cross-border traders or informal vendors, and are drafted with soft, permissive language. Moreover, most of these agreements do not identify specific institutions, procedure, or funding mechanism to implement commitments.

data.objective: Inform gender-responsive trade policy making through data
data.description:
Case story from Canada: an inclusive approach to trade and Gender-based Analysis Plus
Canada's approach: i) extensive collection and analysis of gender disaggregated data; ii) extensive consultations and engagement with under-represented groups; iii) Gender-based Analysis Plus (GBA Plus) methodology supports quantitative and qualitative analysis and helps identify areas for potential new gender responsive and inclusive trade provisions.

GBA Plus in a nutshell: Canada's assessment process considers how diverse groups of women and men experience policies, programmes and initiatives. The "Plus" means that the analysis goes beyond biological (sex) and socio-cultural (gender) differences to consider overlapping identity factors.

Objective of GBA Plus: changing the way Canada develops its trade policy

A Two-Pronged Approach of GBA Plus: i) quantitative analysis: office of Chief Economist conducts an expanded economic impact assessment with a new labour market module and it expands on the traditional Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model. It takes into account gender, age, and the distribution of Canadian workers across eight different occupational groups and 65 sectors of the economy. The data sources used for modelling from Statistics Canada such as Census, Labour Force Survey among others. ii) qualitative analysis: lead trade negotiators conduct GBA Plus on each chapter before negotiations begin and throughout the negotiations, findings inform approach to negotiations and regular updates are conducted before each negotiating round.

Benefits of the GBA Plus Process: i) richer understanding of the impacts and effects of FTAs; ii) supports continuous strengthening and innovating of FTA chapters and implementation of inclusive activities; iii) helps identify new opportunities for mainstreaming new inclusivity and gender responsive provisions in FTAs and committee work; iv) allows for tabling of new provisions in real time at negotiating table; v) identifies gaps in knowledge and areas for more strategic data collection and analysis.

Note: Canada's data collection has focused on women entrepreneurs and has used two broad types of data sets: i) administrative data: hard data capturing the universe of businesses; ii) survey based data: qualitative aspect of the data collection. One key advantage of Canada is the fact that all the data is housed by one agency.

data.objective: Closing the gender gaps could increase GDP by USD 1 trillion in Latin-America alone (Inter American Development Bank). Therefore an inclusive trade policy can contribute to reduce gender gaps.
data.description:
How to build a gender-responsive trade policy

Several tools exist at country level and at the WTO to make a trade policy gender-responsive, such as: i) data on trade and gender; ii) impact assessment of trade on women (Canada and European Union developed methodologies); iii) mainstream a gender focus into trade disciplines; iv) gender responsive trade facilitation and aid for trade; and v) support for women traders.

A specific focus on trade agreements

In recent years, gender provisions in trade agreements have contributed to position gender on the trade agenda. The WTO has identified 257 agreements between 1990 and 2020 which include and implicit or explicit gender provision. Agreements in different regions (e.g. AfCFTA) and plurilateral initiatives such as the Global Trade and Gender Arrangement (GTGA) are addressing gender as a core issue. Increasingly, countries have included stand-alone gender chapters in their trade agreements, which focus on joint commitments on the promotion of gender equality through cooperation. More than addressing specific trade disciplines, the focus of these chapters is on women's economic empowerment and women's rights.
An additional step is to mainstream gender provisions into trade disciplines. This would be a direct means to address gender gaps and inequalities within the trade agreements.

Modalities to mainstream gender provisions in trade disciplines

•Provisions that do not allow for gender discrimination: i) non-discrimination between men and women; and ii) not fail to enforce laws that protect the equality of opportunities for men and women in order to encourage trade or investment;

•Affirmative action to accelerate equality between men and women: i) provisions to further women's empowerment and equal opportunities; and ii) transitory provisions to promote women in trade;
•Reservations for non-conforming measures to protect national legislation and policies that further women's rights and equal opportunities;

•Affirmative action: differential treatment between men and women that is reasonable and objective and aims to achieve a legitimate purpose. Such treatment could establish temporary special measures aimed at accelerating de facto equality between men and women and would not be considered discrimination for the purposes of this provision. An example if such provision is included in the WTO, Joint Initiative on Services Domestic Regulation. Reference Paper on Services Domestic Regulation (INF/SDR/1).

.Sustainable Development in the WTO Reform Agenda:
Trade is an implementing means to achieve the SDGs. SDG 5 (Gender Equality) is a core goal of the Agenda and also a cross-cutting issue within the other SDGs. This needs to be addressed in the WTO reform process.

data.description:
Key results of UNCTAD's publication on "E-commerce from a gender and development perspective":

In 2022, about 66% of the global population used the Internet, with access exceeding 90% in developed countries but only 36% in least developed countries (LDCs), reflecting lower network coverage, particularly in rural areas. Affordability also remains a major barrier, as mobile broadband costs represent a much higher share of income in LDCs compared to developed and other developing countries.

Between and within country digital divides: Internet access is shaped by geographical factors that influence coverage and by income levels that determine the affordability of devices and subscriptions. However, coverage does not guarantee use, as illustrated by LDCs where around 80% of the population has coverage but only 36% actually uses the Internet. Moreover, Internet use does not necessarily lead to safe, productive, or meaningful outcomes.

Development and gender digital divides: In developed countries, the digital gender gap is nearly closed, with over 90% of both women and men using the Internet. In contrast, the gap remains large in LDCs, where only 30% of women versus 43% of men are online, highlighting compounded digital disadvantages for women.

Opportunities for women-led small enterprises: Digital tools and online platforms lower entry costs, connect entrepreneurs directly with buyers and suppliers, and expand access to information, knowledge, and skills. They also enhance flexibility, reduce mobility and safety constraints, enable entry into new sectors, support the services economy where many women work, and proved vital for business survival during the pandemic.

Access to tools to trade online: In LDCs, the number of people who have a mobile money account is quite high. And this is linked to the fact that many people are unbanked, don't have access to proper official financial institutions.

Obstacles: women entrepreneurs face compounded disadvantages at every stage: limited access to technology and the Internet, lower education and digital skills, and reduced start-up capital and access to finance. These gaps result in women-led businesses being smaller, less profitable, and concentrated in low-value sectors, with rural women in LDCs being particularly disadvantaged.

Digital platforms: Business platforms can boost visibility, increase demand, reduce search and information costs, and offer additional services. However, concerns include usage costs, limited bargaining power for MSMEs, data control issues, and potential algorithmic disadvantages for small businesses. Social platforms
data.policy_outcome:
Policy recommendations: E-commerce presents significant opportunities for women’s economic empowerment, but digital access and benefits are unequally distributed between countries and between women and men, particularly in developing nations. Gender gaps both reinforce and are reinforced by digital gaps, limiting the performance of women-led e-commerce businesses. Key areas to address include gender discrimination in education, STEM, access to credit, and discriminatory laws.

Policies to overcome gender barriers in e-commerce include creating women-friendly digital platforms, providing training and advocacy, analysing informal online commerce, forming partnerships, ensuring access to information, collecting gender-disaggregated data, and incorporating gender perspectives in e-commerce negotiations. Addressing these barriers is key to inclusive recovery and sustainable development post-pandemic.

data.description: The research examines whether and how trade agreements can empower women with disabilities and reduce barriers to their economic participation, noting that trade policies can both reduce and exacerbate inequalities if inclusion is not considered. The study finds that women with disabilities face heightened barriers in employment, access to resources, healthcare, infrastructure, and protection from discrimination, and that trade agreements can help address these challenges if they include targeted, enforceable commitments. • Patents can help women inventors, secure funding, which can aid in commercializing an invention to bring it to market. Similarly, inventions designed for women, by any gender inventor, can empower women by making their lives easier or better. In addition, in some cases, holding a patent is a sign of professional success, and can help a woman advance in her field, get a promotion, or a higher-paying job. This may be particularly helpful for women in male-dominated career fields.
• Trademarks help women-owned businesses identify their goods and services. This can help establish a "brand" which consumers recognize and seek out. Once consumers begin to recognize a brand, they may develop loyalty to it, which may lead to more sales of a product or service. It can also lead to licensing agreements and other such partnerships with sellers, as we'll see in an example later on.
• Copyright can help women artists protect and obtain compensation for their music and other artwork.
• Some recommendations: there still exists a significant gender gap with respect to women's participation in the IP system. Improving women's participation in IP would improve not only their own earnings but also economic growth. Many countries, along with the World Intellectual Property Organization, are seeking to promote women's participation in innovation and science and technology. Increasing awareness of the benefits to women of using the IP system is an important factor in increasing this participation.

data.instrument: Policy dialogue for International Day of Women in Diplomacy
data.objective: Promote women's access to decision making and leadership roles and positions
data.description:
The panel discussion on gender equity and mentorship in trade diplomacy emphasized the positive correlation between diverse leadership and improved economic outcomes. While challenges remain, particularly around engaging men in gender equity discussions, the panel highlighted the importance of mentorship and sponsorship in advancing underrepresented groups. Key advice for young women included building confidence, resilience, and education, as well as asserting their achievements. Practical steps for greater engagement involved fostering inclusive discussions, promoting mentorship, and encouraging the active support of allies to enhance gender diversity in leadership roles.

For more details

The panel discussion highlighted the critical intersection of gender equity, mentorship, and effective trade diplomacy. It emphasized that while gender diversity in leadership roles correlates positively with better economic outcomes and successful trade negotiations, significant challenges remain in achieving balanced participation and effective mentorship.

• Gender Equity and Economic Performance

The discussion underscored that gender diversity in leadership is not just a matter of fairness but also of economic effectiveness. Research and real-world examples show a strong correlation between having diverse leadership and achieving superior economic performance. Diverse perspectives in decision-making processes lead to more innovative solutions and successful trade outcomes. This correlation serves as a powerful argument for increasing gender diversity at the highest levels of trade diplomacy.

• Challenges in Inclusive Discussions

One of the key challenges discussed was the varying perceptions of gender equity and the underrepresentation of men in these discussions. The panel suggested that engaging men who are already supportive of gender equity can be an effective strategy for bringing more individuals into the conversation. By having committed allies advocate for gender equity and mentor others, progress can be made in aligning perceptions and increasing overall participation in these critical discussions.

• The Role of Mentorship and Sponsorship

Mentorship emerged as a crucial element for advancing careers in trade diplomacy. The panel emphasized the importance of both women and men acting as mentors to guide and support emerging professionals. Sponsorship, where senior figures advocate for the career advancement of individuals from underrepresented groups, was highlighted as equally important. Effective sponsorship involves not only mentoring but also actively promoting individuals for new opportunities and leadership roles.

•Advice for the Next Generation

Panellists provided valuable advice for young women aspiring to careers in trade diplomacy.

Key recommendations included:

o Confidence: Believe in your abilities and maintain self-confidence. Success in diplomacy requires a strong sense of self and the conviction that you can achieve your goals.

o Resilience and Proactivity: Be resilient in the face of challenges and proactively seek opportunities for growth and development. Continuous learning and skill enhancement are essential for career advancement.

o Education: Invest in education to gain the necessary knowledge and skills for success. Education empowers individuals to navigate the complexities of trade diplomacy and leadership.

o Taking Up Space: Do not shy away from asserting your achievements and capabilities. Making your successes known and advocating for yourself can help ensure recognition and advancement.

• Practical Steps for Greater Engagement

The panel discussed practical steps to foster greater engagement in gender equity efforts. Meeting individuals where they are in their understanding of gender issues and gradually guiding them toward more inclusive practices was deemed effective. Additionally, building robust professional networks and seeking mentorship—both formal and informal—were highlighted as key strategies for career development and advocacy.

data.description:
Presentation of the CEDAW General Recommendation No. 40 (GR40), which aims to support CEDAW members in implementing their commitments to ensure equal and inclusive representation of women in leadership positions.

GR40 advocates for 50:50 gender parity in all decision-making systems as a fundamental right and essential for inclusive and sustainable governance.

GR40 highlights the need to remove systemic barriers that limit women’s participation in leadership roles and promotes transformative reforms in sectors including economic and trade systems.

The recommendation emphasizes the importance of moving beyond a 30% representation threshold, aiming for full gender parity in both public and private sectors. It also calls for the implementation of policies and recruitment strategies to address intersectional discrimination and to ensure equal representation.

GR40 further proposes temporary measures such as quotas to enhance women’s leadership in key areas like STEM, trade negotiations, and executive positions.

The recommendation also stresses the need for gender-sensitive trade policies and advocates for greater participation of women in technology and innovation sectors.

The Philippines: Gender and Development training workshop for rural women entrepreneurs titled "Her Route to Foreign Markets"

The Philippines presented its experience in implementing a gender-responsive capacity-building initiative for women entrepreneurs under its national Gender and Development (GAD) framework. It highlighted a training workshop titled Her Route to Foreign Markets, held in September 2025 in Lapu-Lapu City, Cebu, and organized by the Philippine Mission to the WTO in collaboration with the WTO Trade and Gender Office. Targeting rural women entrepreneurs, particularly in the tourism and agriculture sectors, the workshop aimed to strengthen the capacity of women-owned and women-led micro and small enterprises to navigate multilateral trade rules and engage in export markets. This was the first WTO-supported training of its kind conducted in the Philippines using a gender lens.

The Philippines explained that the initiative forms part of its GAD programme, anchored in the Magna Carta of Women, which mandates the integration of gender equality across government policies, programmes and budgets, including the allocation of dedicated funding for gender-related activities. It underlined that its trade-related GAD initiatives contribute to national constitutional commitments and international obligations, including the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 5 on gender equality.

The workshop brought together experts from the WTO Trade and Gender Office, APEC, national trade and agriculture authorities, financial institutions, academia and international organizations. Sessions covered value chains in tourism and agriculture, international trade rules, market access, free trade agreements, access to finance and export strategies. Discussions emphasized the role of women as drivers of inclusive growth and the importance of continuous learning, trade literacy and gender-responsive trade policy.

Key outcomes included the identification of priority areas for future capacity building, strengthened inter-agency coordination and practical support to help women entrepreneurs scale up and enter export markets. Participants highlighted persistent challenges, including limited access to finance, complex trade rules and weak market networks, and called for stronger ecosystems through whole-of-government and private sector approaches. Recommendations included institutionalizing trade literacy, translating trade agreements into local languages, linking finance with market access and improving gender-responsive trade data.

The Philippines reported strong positive feedback from participants, who expressed increased confidence in applying the skills acquired and interest in follow-up trainings. It concluded by indicating its intention to replicate the initiative in other regions, in continued cooperation with the WTO Trade and Gender Office, as part of its ongoing GAD programme.
data.policy_outcome:
Programme evaluation summary

• Overall satisfaction was very high: 100% of participants felt the objectives were clear, and would recommend the training to other entrepreneurs.

• Strong relevance and quality: 75% rated the content, delivery, materials, and format as very relevant/effective; the remaining participants rated them as appropriate or valuable.

• Effective facilitation: 88% rated trainers as highly effective, 100% agreed trainers were knowledgeable, and most felt participation and engagement were well encouraged.

• High practical impact: All participants felt confident applying the knowledge and skills gained, particularly in export planning, trade policies, FTAs, financing, and business scaling.

• Most valued elements: Sessions 1, 4, 8, and 9; real-life case studies, guest entrepreneur insights, and topics on trade policies, tariffs, market access, and export terminology.

• Areas for improvement: Participants suggested more case studies, deeper coverage of export pricing, policies, digital tools, and support services, as well as longer duration and greater inclusion of women entrepreneurs.

• Future demand: Strong interest in follow-up and future WTO-related trainings, reflecting the program’s perceived relevance and usefulness.

data.objective: Advancing inclusive trade policymaking
data.description:
The SheTrades Outlook tool, developed through the UK-funded SheTrades Commonwealth programme, is designed to help policymakers and women’s business associations assess and improve the policy environment for women in business and trade.

The UK onboarded ITC's SheTrades Outlook tool in 2023. The process required inputs from 15 government departments and external stakeholders and involved several months of data collection.

Areas where further progress is possible: improving women’s participation in consultation processes, adopting international definitions of women-owned and women-led businesses, and strengthening the collection of gender-disaggregated data.

Process: at the end of the review, the UK noted and ITC co-hosted a validation workshop that reviewed the results, discussed policy gaps and examined opportunities for reform, including better visibility of training opportunities, greater coordination with devolved governments and improving conditions for women with caring responsibilities.
data.policy_outcome:
The United Kingdom’s assessment showed the country’s strong performance in integrating gender equality into trade agreements and impact assessments, including in the UK–India FTA, and in using gender indicators for trade policy, such as in the UK trade strategy.

The government has also established a trade and gender focal point within the Department for Business and Trade.

The exercise strengthened collaboration across government and helped promote gender-responsive approaches within trade and the wider economy.

The UK continues to work through the SheTrades Outlook network to exchange experiences with other countries and to support the ongoing implementation of recommendations aimed at advancing gender equality in trade.
data.outcome_data: ITC noted that SheTrades Outlook has now been rolled out in 64 countries, with 51 onboarded through funding from the United Kingdom.

data.objective: Promote gender equality in development programmes
data.description:
The UNDP's Strategic Plan 2026–2029 identifies gender equality as a major driver for achieving its four objectives: prosperity for all, effective governance, crisis resilience, and a healthy planet.

Alongside digital transformation and sustainable finance, gender equality is presented as an accelerator intended to multiply progress across UNDP’s work on sustainable development.

UNDP underlined that gender equality also remains a goal in its own right and stressed the importance of avoiding the risk of dilution that can accompany mainstreaming.

Selected high impact areas will be prioritised and that gender equality work will continue to be led by specialised expertise, including gender equality experts.
data.policy_outcome: UNDP is developing a new gender equality strategy, which is expected to focus on areas such as expanding care systems, fiscal policies for gender equality, and women’s leadership across sectors. UNDP invited members of the IWG to share views on priorities for advancing gender equality, particularly in trade and development, as well as on the role UNDP should play. The strategy is expected to be presented in June 2026.

data.description:
Nigeria is among the first four pilot countries alongside the Dominican Republic, Jordan, and Mongolia to benefit from the widest fund.

Nigerian Export Promotion Council was selected as the National Business Support Organization partner for implementation and played a key role in delivering a highly successful open call for applications campaign.

The campaign, held from 22 April to 18 May 2025, attracted over 68,000 applications from Nigerian women entrepreneurs, reflecting both the strong entrepreneurial spirit of Nigerian women and the relevance of this program. following a rigorous selection process.

146 women-led businesses were selected for support.

129 under the Discovery Grant designed to help entrepreneurs build foundational Digital and export skills with support of US$5,000 and under the booster grant targeting more advanced businesses ready to scale their digital trade capabilities with support of up to US$30,000.

The official high-level launch event took place in Abuja on 14 of August, 2025, bringing together women entrepreneurs, government representatives, international organizations, and the private sector.

Beyond financial support, the WEIDE Fund offers mentorship, training, and access to networks, helping women-led SMEs move from local to global market. The training component was launched during the Abuja event and hosted by Nigeria Export Promotion Council, where beneficiaries met their trainers and began workshops over two days. The full training program spans 12 months. These sessions aim to strengthen participants' digital literacy, e-commerce skills and access to the global market, helping build sustainable competitiveness for Nigerian women-led businesses.

Nigeria views the White Day Fund as a concrete demonstration of how trade can serve as a catalyst for gender equality, digital inclusion and inclusive economic growth.

This partnership supports Nigeria's broader national priorities on women, economic empowerment, digital innovation, and job creation.

data.objective: Promote research on trade and gender
data.description:
The research event brought together policymakers, researchers, and international organisations to explore how trade policy can drive women’s economic empowerment. Discussions underscored the need to treat gender equality as a core element of trade policy, not a secondary concern.

Key themes included the opportunities and challenges of digitalisation, the role of regional trade agreements, and the importance of gender-disaggregated data. The United Kingdom, Brazil, Chile, New Zealand, and others shared national experiences, while institutional initiatives from ITC, FAO, and the World Bank highlighted efforts to make trade systems more inclusive.
